flashcards.note: Bad news does not improve with age, and softening it until it misleads destroys trust.

flashcards.back: Useful information picked up by overhearing colleagues who sit together. Distributed teams lose it and must replace it deliberately.
flashcards.note: Recorded decisions and open channels are common replacements.

flashcards.back: Explicit knowledge can be written down and shared through documents. Tacit knowledge is judgement and experience, and transfers mainly through people working together.
flashcards.note: A handover of documents alone loses the tacit knowledge.

flashcards.back: Turn lessons into defaults the next project uses, such as checklists, estimating guides, risk templates and standards.
flashcards.note: Repositories capture lessons; defaults get them used.

flashcards.back: Pair others with the expert on real work, record the reasoning behind decisions, and start before the person leaves.
flashcards.note: Teams that rotate work and pair regularly rarely depend on one person.

flashcards.back: The allowed variation from plan before a decision must be escalated. Within it the project manager manages; when a forecast breaches it, escalate promptly.
flashcards.note: Waiting until a breach is certain before warning anyone shrinks the options.

flashcards.front: Splitting a change to stay under a threshold
flashcards.back: Breaking one change into smaller ones so each avoids the approval it would need as a whole. It defeats the purpose of governance.
flashcards.note: Respect a threshold's purpose, not just its letter.

flashcards.back: Set boundaries, outcomes and review points rather than approving each change. The product owner decides inside the boundaries.
flashcards.note: Item-by-item approval suits fixed scope, not daily backlog change.

flashcards.back: Use a fast, agreed route rather than no route, then record the change and take it through the full process retrospectively.
flashcards.note: If emergencies become routine, the normal process or the planning needs fixing.

flashcards.front: Where change control sits in agile work
flashcards.back: Scope change enters the backlog and is ranked by the product owner; the sprint goal is protected; changes to budget, dates or contracts still go to governance.
flashcards.note: Agile moves much of change control into the backlog rather than removing it.

flashcards.front: Contents of a change impact assessment
flashcards.back: Effects on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and resources, the hidden work such as testing and compliance, the cost of not changing, and the options.
flashcards.note: Track an approved change too; bring it back if its real cost grows well beyond the assessment.

flashcards.back: Names the cause, the uncertain event and its effect on an objective, and has a named owner.
flashcards.note: Vague entries such as supplier issues cannot be analysed or owned.

flashcards.front: Signs of a stale risk register
flashcards.back: Ratings unchanged for months, most risks scored the same, no owners, and passed risks never retired.
flashcards.note: A stale register gives false comfort, which is worse than having none.

flashcards.back: Start the planned response, confirm the facts, update the register and check whether related risks have changed.
flashcards.note: Recording that a trigger fired without acting on it defeats its purpose.

flashcards.back: A risk might happen. An issue has happened and needs action. An impediment is anything slowing or stopping the team's work now.
flashcards.note: Recording a current blocker as a risk delays the action it needs.

flashcards.front: Clearing a blocker at the right level
flashcards.back: The team clears what it can; the scrum master or project manager clears what the team cannot; escalate only what they cannot clear either.
flashcards.note: A blocker left for a week costs a week of the team's time.

flashcards.back: Find its cause, often a process or policy outside the team, and work with that process's owner, using evidence of the cost.
flashcards.note: Working round a recurring blocker each time pays its cost indefinitely.

flashcards.back: Evidence is produced as the work happens, dated, attributable and linked to the requirement. Claims are statements that compliance exists.
flashcards.note: A signed checklist proves someone signed it, not that the checks were done well.

flashcards.back: Record obligations as testable requirements with owners, add them to the definition of done, and involve specialists early.
flashcards.note: Retrofitting compliance to a finished product is slow and sometimes impossible.

flashcards.back: Understand it with the specialist, contain any immediate harm, plan the fix through the proper route, and follow any duty to report.
flashcards.note: Concealment usually costs far more than the gap itself.

flashcards.back: Continuous improvement through many small changes made by the people doing the work, rather than occasional large reforms.
flashcards.note: The habit of improving matters more than any single change.

flashcards.back: A map of every step from request to delivery that separates time spent working from time spent waiting.
flashcards.note: Waiting usually dominates, so that is where the biggest gains are.

flashcards.back: Few in number, each with one named owner, a stated expected result and a date to check whether it worked.
flashcards.note: Long lists and actions owned by the whole team are repeated, not completed.

flashcards.back: Delivery puts the result in place. Adoption is people actually changing how they work. Benefits arrive only with adoption.
flashcards.note: Measure adoption by behaviour, not by training completed or go-live dates.

flashcards.back: Publicly supporting a change while keeping the old way alive in practice, often from fear of losing control, status or skills.
flashcards.note: Read resistance from behaviour as well as words, and talk to people directly.

flashcards.front: Evidence that a change has been adopted
flashcards.back: The old way has largely stopped, and people are using the new way well, for example with falling error rates.
flashcards.note: Training records and on-time go-live measure inputs, not adoption.

flashcards.back: An uncertain change, such as a proposal under consultation, is a risk to monitor with triggers. A certain change, such as an announced rule with a date, is a requirement to plan.
flashcards.note: Treating an announced change as a risk delays planning it.

flashcards.back: Regularly review political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors, with named people watching the areas that matter most.
flashcards.note: Scan as often as the environment actually changes.

flashcards.back: Track the versions of third-party services and platforms you rely on, when support ends and what the alternatives are.
flashcards.note: Plan for a known end date even if it falls after the project closes.

glossary.d: The conditions a deliverable must satisfy before the customer will sign for it. Written per item and agreed before the work starts, which is what separates them from a definition of done.
Deliverables the customer has formally signed off in Validate Scope. Verified deliverables become accepted ones; the reverse never happens.
How close a measurement is to the true value. Distinct from precision, which is how tightly repeated measurements cluster; a set of readings can be precise and consistently wrong.
The executing process that gets people, equipment and materials actually assigned to the project, usually by negotiation with the managers who control them.
Attending to a speaker closely enough to reflect back what was meant rather than what was said. The tool behind most correct answers in stakeholder conflict scenarios.
A distinct piece of scheduled work, decomposed from a work package. The schedule is built from activities; the WBS is built from deliverables.
The detail attached to each activity: predecessors, successors, leads, lags, resource requirements, constraints and assumptions.
The complete set of scheduled activities, with enough description that whoever performs one knows what it means.
What has genuinely been spent on the work that earned value measures. No ceiling and no budget rate applied.
An approach where requirements emerge and work is delivered in frequent small increments. Suits volatile requirements and available customer feedback.
The final Tuckman stage, where the work finishes and the team disperses. Recognition and lessons capture belong here.
Groups a large number of ideas into natural clusters for review. Common in requirements workshops and retrospectives.
In SAFe, a long-lived team of agile teams that plans and delivers together on a shared cadence.
Any document binding the parties, most often a contract. An agreement is an input to charter development when the project comes from an external customer.
Evaluating identified options against criteria before choosing. Appears as a tool in more processes than almost anything else.
Estimating by scaling from a similar past project or activity. Fast, cheap and the least accurate; used when detail is not yet available.
Something taken to be true for planning purposes without proof. Every assumption is a risk in disguise and belongs in the assumption log.
The register of assumptions and constraints, opened in Develop Project Charter and maintained for the life of the project.
A structured independent review of whether a process is being followed and is fit for purpose. Audits examine processes; inspections examine products.
One person decides for the group. Fast, appropriate in emergencies, and costly in commitment when used routinely.
The threat response that eliminates the risk entirely, usually by changing the plan so the exposure no longer exists.
An ordered list of everything currently known to be wanted in a product. Ordered, not prioritised into buckets: exactly one item is next.
The continuous activity of adding detail, estimates and order to backlog items. Not a Scrum event, and typically around ten percent of the team's capacity.
Working from the end of the network to the start to calculate late start and late finish dates. Combined with the forward pass it yields float.
A structure where authority is genuinely shared between project and functional managers. Team members report to two people, which is the source of most matrix conflict.
A schedule presentation with activities on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal. Good for communicating dates, poor for showing dependencies.
An approved version of a plan artefact, changed only through formal change control, against which actual performance is measured.
The documentation supporting an estimate: how it was derived, what it assumes, what it excludes and the confidence range around it.
Comparing practices or results against a comparable organisation to identify improvements and set targets.
How and when the benefits in the business case will be delivered and measured. Often outlives the project itself.
The documents inviting seller responses. RFI seeks information, RFQ seeks a price, RFP seeks a proposed solution, IFB seeks a sealed bid.
A meeting with all prospective sellers so every one of them hears the same questions answered at the same time. Fairness is the entire point.
Estimating each low-level component and rolling the results up. The most accurate technique and the most expensive to produce.
Generating a large number of ideas without evaluating them, then evaluating separately. Merging the two phases kills the first.
The total authorised budget for the work, which is the cost baseline summed to the end. Excludes management reserve.
Remaining work plotted against time. Falls toward zero; a flat line is work not being finished rather than work not being started.
Completed work plotted against a total scope line. Shows scope growth, which a burndown hides.
The justification for the investment: the problem, the options, the expected benefit and the cost. Re-tested when assumptions change, not filed at initiation.
The net quantifiable benefit an organisation gets from the project. May be financial, social, or an enabling capability.
The rhythm at which something recurs: a sprint length, a release interval, a review frequency. A stable cadence is what makes planning possible without detailed prediction.
A tool that traces an observed effect back through categories of possible cause. Used in root cause analysis.
The group with authority to approve or reject change requests. Its composition and authority are defined in the change management plan.
The record of every change request and its disposition, including the rejected ones. Rejections are the part people forget to record.
How changes will be requested, assessed, decided and implemented, and who sits on the board.
A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline. Covers corrective action, preventive action, defect repair and updates.
The document that authorises the project and names the project manager with authority to apply resources. Issued by a sponsor outside the project.
A structured list used to verify that a required set of steps has been performed. Effective precisely because it does not rely on memory.
The handling of contested changes where buyer and seller disagree on compensation. Negotiation is always the first route; the contract's dispute mechanism is the fallback.
The single closing process. Confirms acceptance, settles contracts, releases resources and archives what was learned. Happens even when a project is cancelled.
The process group with one process, concerned with finishing or abandoning work in an orderly way.
Developing capability by asking rather than telling. The default leadership mode where there is time; instruction is for when there is not.
The professional standard covering responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty. Its clauses are the tiebreaker in ethics scenarios.
The conflict mode that works the underlying issue to a solution both parties own. Highest-scoring answer where time and relationship permit.
The planning process that determines and documents stakeholder needs in a form specific enough to test against.
Putting the team in one physical place to raise the bandwidth of communication. A virtual equivalent needs deliberate design to approach it.
The number of possible pairwise links in a group, equal to n(n-1)/2. Grows quadratically, which is the arithmetic argument for small teams.
Who needs what information, in what format, how often, through what channel, and from whom.
The conflict mode where both parties give something up for a workable middle. Produces a settlement, not necessarily a solution.

Control over the characteristics of a product and its documentation, including version identification and status accounting. Distinct from change control, which decides whether a change happens at all.
Handling disagreement so it produces a decision rather than damage. The five modes are collaborate, compromise, smooth, force and withdraw.
Meeting the stated requirements. Cost of conformance covers prevention and appraisal; cost of nonconformance covers internal and external failure.
A limiting factor on how the project can be executed: a fixed date, a capped budget, a mandated technology, a regulatory requirement.
Money or time inside the cost or schedule baseline, set aside for identified risks. The project manager may spend it without a change request.
A response prepared in advance and executed only if a defined trigger occurs. The trigger must be specified or the plan cannot fire.
Merging and verifying work many times a day so integration defects are found while they are still small.
A management control point in the WBS where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and compared to earned value.
Plots a process measure over time against control limits derived from the process itself. Signals whether variation is normal or something has changed.
The monitoring and controlling process that tracks spend against the cost baseline and forecasts the outturn.
Boundaries calculated from the process, typically three standard deviations from the mean. Not the same as specification limits, which come from the customer.
Managing the seller relationship, monitoring contract performance, handling claims, making payments and closing the procurement out.
Inspecting deliverables and measurements to confirm conformance. Produces verified deliverables, which Validate Scope then takes to the customer.
Ensuring physical resources are available as planned and used as planned. People are handled in Manage Team, not here.
Tracking progress against the schedule baseline, forecasting completion, and managing changes to the baseline.
Monitoring the scope baseline and managing every change to it through the proper channel. Scope creep and gold plating are its failure modes.
An action that realigns future performance with the plan. Distinct from preventive action, which addresses a risk that has not yet materialised.
The approved time-phased budget, excluding management reserve but including contingency. Changed only through formal change control.
The total cost of achieving conformance plus the cost of failing to. Prevention is cheaper than appraisal, and appraisal far cheaper than failure.
EV divided by AC. Below 1.0 means the work completed cost more than it was budgeted at. Historically it rarely recovers.
Costs reimbursed plus a fee awarded on the buyer's subjective assessment of performance, usually not subject to appeal.
Costs reimbursed plus a fee fixed at the outset. The buyer carries the cost risk; the seller's profit does not move with cost.
Costs reimbursed plus a fee that varies with performance against a target, sharing the over- or under-run at an agreed ratio.
EV minus AC. Negative means over cost. A variance in money, where the index is a ratio.
Compressing the schedule by adding resources to critical path activities. Always adds cost, and its effect diminishes fast.
A scheduling approach that places buffers at the end of chains rather than padding individual activities, and manages resource constraints explicitly.
The longest path through the network, and therefore the shortest possible duration. Activities on it have zero total float, and there can be more than one.
A team with every skill needed to deliver a usable increment without depending on another team.
A stacked area chart of work in each state over time. A widening band marks a bottleneck long before a date is missed.
Elapsed time from work starting on an item to it being finished. Always less than or equal to lead time.
A fifteen-minute event for the developers to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and re-plan the day. Not a status report to a manager.
The family of techniques that turn observations into conclusions: variance, trend, root cause, alternatives, cost-benefit and the rest.
A diagram of choices, chance events and their values, solved backwards to find the option with the best expected monetary value.
Breaking work into smaller components until each can be estimated and managed with confidence. Produces the WBS, then the activity list.
A change request category: correcting a nonconforming component. Distinct from corrective and preventive action.
The planning process that decomposes work packages into the specific actions needed to produce them.
The planning process that turns collected requirements into a precise description of project and product scope, including exclusions.
The team-wide quality standard an increment must meet to be considered releasable. Applies to every item; acceptance criteria apply to one.
An optional agreement about when a backlog item is well enough understood to be pulled into a sprint. Useful as a guide, harmful as a gate.
Any unique and verifiable product, result or capability that a process, phase or project must produce.
Anonymous rounds of expert input with feedback between rounds, converging without the loudest voice dominating.
A logical relationship between activities. Mandatory dependencies are inherent in the work; discretionary ones are a choice and are the first thing revisited when compressing.
The planning process that aggregates cost estimates into an authorised, time-phased cost baseline.
The initiating process that produces the charter and formally authorises the project.
The planning process that integrates all subsidiary plans and baselines into one approved document.
The planning process that combines sequence, durations and resources into a schedule model and baselines it.
The executing process that improves competence, interaction and the overall environment so the team performs better.
The executing process that performs the planned work and implements approved changes. The only source of deliverables and of work performance data.
A sequencing choice based on preference or best practice rather than necessity. Also called preferred or soft logic.
Elapsed working time for an activity. Effort is person-hours; the two are related by the number of resources and are not interchangeable.
The earliest an activity can finish given the network logic. Calculated in the forward pass.
The earliest an activity can start given the network logic. Calculated in the forward pass.
The budgeted cost of the work actually completed. Progress valued at the plan, never at what it cost.
A method that integrates scope, schedule and cost into a single set of measures by valuing completed work at its budget.
The labour required for an activity, expressed in person-hours or person-days. Independent of how many people are applied.
Recognising and regulating one's own emotions and reading them in others. Underpins most of the interpersonal tools in Manage Team.
The opportunity response that increases probability or positive impact. The mirror of mitigate.
Conditions the project must work within and cannot change: culture, governance, regulations, market conditions, existing systems.
The response, available for both threats and opportunities, that transfers ownership to someone outside the project with the authority to act. Once accepted, it leaves the project register.
The planning process that estimates the working periods each activity needs given its assigned resources.
The planning process that determines the types and quantities of people, equipment and materials each activity needs.
The forecast total cost of the project. The default form, BAC divided by CPI, assumes current cost performance continues.
The planning process that develops an approximation of the money needed to complete each piece of work.
The forecast cost of the remaining work. EAC minus AC in the ordinary case.
Probability multiplied by impact, summed across outcomes. Threats carry a negative value and opportunities a positive one.
Input from people with demonstrated knowledge of the subject. Listed as a tool in nearly every process, and rarely the discriminating answer on its own.
The opportunity response that makes the opportunity certain to occur. The mirror of avoid.
A relationship between a project activity and something outside the project's control, such as a permit or a supplier's delivery.
An agile method centred on engineering discipline: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring and small releases.
Compressing the schedule by overlapping activities that were planned in sequence. Adds risk and rework rather than cost.
A piece of functionality that delivers value to a user, typically larger than a story and smaller than an epic.
The 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 scale often used for story points. The widening gaps reflect that large estimates are less precise, which is the point.
One agreed price regardless of the seller's actual costs. The seller carries the cost risk; suits well-defined stable scope.
See cause-and-effect diagram. Traces an effect back through categories of possible cause.
A fixed price with an incentive tied to performance against a target, subject to a ceiling price. Above the point of total assumption the seller absorbs all further cost.

glossary.t: Fixed price with economic price adjustment
glossary.d: A fixed price indexed to a published financial measure. Used for multi-year work exposed to inflation or currency movement.
How long an activity can slip. Total float is against the project finish; free float is against the earliest start of its successor.
A diagram of the steps in a process and the decisions between them. Used to expose where defects can be introduced.
The conflict mode that imposes one view. Appropriate in emergencies and safety matters; corrosive as a habit.
An estimate of future conditions based on current performance. EAC, ETC and VAC are the cost forecasts.
The first Tuckman stage: polite, tentative, and dependent on the leader for direction.
Working from the start of the network to the end to calculate early start and early finish dates.
How long an activity can slip without delaying the early start of any immediate successor.
A structure organised by specialism, where the functional manager controls the resources and the project manager has little or no authority.
Adjusting the schedule of work so planned expenditure stays within the funding available in each period.
The team adding features nobody asked for. A scope failure and a quality failure at once, and never a correct answer.
A category assigned to items with the same functional use but different technical characteristics. Low grade is acceptable; low quality is not.
Explicit expectations about how the team will behave, agreed with the team rather than imposed on it.
A bar chart of how frequently each range of values occurs, showing the shape of a distribution.
Records from previous projects held as an organisational process asset and used for estimating and risk identification.
Combining predictive and adaptive elements within one project, typically by component, by phase, or by separating governance from delivery.
The planning process that finds individual risks and sources of overall risk, and records them in enough detail to act on. Iterative and never finished.
The initiating process that finds everyone who can affect or be affected by the project and records their interest, influence and impact.
Anything blocking the team's progress. Removing them is the scrum master's principal work.
The executing process that actually carries out agreed responses. Added because registers full of unexecuted responses were the commonest failure.
Delivery in usable pieces where the requirements are largely known. Each increment adds function to something already working.
The buyer's own estimate of what a procurement should cost, prepared as a benchmark against seller pricing.
A graphical representation of decisions, uncertainties and outcomes and the influences between them.
A large, visible, low-effort display of project state, placed where the team and its stakeholders will see it without asking.
The process group containing Develop Project Charter and Identify Stakeholders. Answers whether the project may start and who it is for.
Examining a product against its requirements. Used in Control Quality internally and in Validate Scope with the customer.
The single point at which all change requests are reviewed and decided, so that a change accepted in one area is reflected in every other.
The discount rate at which a project's net present value is zero. Higher is better when comparing investments.
A bid document seeking sealed price bids for a well-specified scope, usually awarded on price alone.
Requirements refined through repeated cycles of work, with delivery typically at the end rather than each cycle.
A current problem that requires action. A risk is a future uncertainty; an issue has already happened.
The record of issues, their owners, status and resolution. Distinct from the risk register in tense as much as in content.
Continuous incremental improvement made by the people doing the work, rather than improvement imposed as a programme.
A flow method that visualises work, limits work in progress and improves an existing process by evolution. No prescribed roles or timeboxes.
A visual model of the workflow with a column per state and explicit WIP limits. Queues between stages are where the delay actually lives.
The meeting that aligns the team and stakeholders on purpose, roles and approach at the start of a project or phase.
A deliberate delay inserted between a predecessor and its successor. Waiting for concrete to cure is a lag, not an activity.
The latest an activity can finish without delaying the project. Calculated in the backward pass.
The latest an activity can start without delaying the project. Calculated in the backward pass.
An overlap that lets a successor start before its predecessor finishes. Negative lag, and a form of fast tracking.
Elapsed time from the customer's request to delivery. Always at least the cycle time, because it includes queue time before work starts.
Influencing people toward a goal. A set of behaviours available to anyone, distinct from the authority a position confers.
A body of practice focused on maximising value and eliminating waste, from which much of Kanban's thinking derives.
Opened early and updated throughout, recording what worked and what did not. Archived into the repository at closure.
The organisation's accumulated store of lessons across projects, held as an organisational process asset.
Support work that has no discrete deliverable of its own and is measured by time elapsed rather than by output.
For a stable system, cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput. The mathematical case for limiting WIP.
Deciding whether to produce something internally or procure it, weighing cost, capability, capacity and risk.
Budget held outside the cost baseline for unknown-unknowns. Requires a change request and management approval to access.
The executing process that creates, distributes, stores and disposes of project information as the plan requires.
The executing process that uses existing organisational knowledge and captures new knowledge while the people who gained it are still available.
The executing process that audits the process and improves it. Preventive, where Control Quality is detective.
The executing process of communicating and working with stakeholders to meet expectations, address concerns and build support.
The executing process that tracks performance, gives feedback, resolves issues and manages changes to optimise the team.
A relationship inherent in the nature of the work, sometimes called hard logic. Cannot be removed to compress a schedule.
A structure where team members report both to a functional manager and to a project manager. Weak, balanced and strong describe how the authority splits.
A significant point in the schedule with zero duration. Marking one does not consume time.
The threat response that reduces probability or impact to an acceptable level without eliminating the risk.
The monitoring process that tracks overall progress, consumes work performance information and emits work performance reports.
The monitoring process that checks information is reaching people and having the intended effect. Monitor rather than Control because comprehension cannot be compelled.
The monitoring process that tracks identified risks, watches for new ones and evaluates whether responses are working.
The monitoring process that watches relationships and adjusts engagement strategies as levels shift.
Running a schedule or cost model thousands of times with sampled inputs to produce a distribution of outcomes and a confidence level for any date or figure.
The realistic estimate in a three-point technique, given expected resources and expected productivity.
What makes people apply discretionary effort. Herzberg's split between hygiene factors and motivators is the one most often tested.
Scoring options against weighted criteria to produce a ranked comparison rather than an argued preference.
Reaching agreement through discussion. The first route for a contract claim and the principal tool for acquiring resources in a matrix.
The value of future cash flows discounted to today, minus the investment. Positive means the project is worth doing at that discount rate.
A representation of activities and their logical relationships. The basis for the forward and backward passes.
Brainstorming followed by structured ranking or voting, so that the loudest contributor does not determine the outcome.
The third Tuckman stage, where working agreements settle and trust builds.
Watching people do the work to elicit requirements they cannot articulate. Effective where the process is habitual.
A risk with a positive effect on objectives. Handled with the same rigour as a threat, using escalate, exploit, share, enhance or accept.
The best-case estimate in a three-point technique, assuming everything goes well.
Plans, processes, templates and knowledge repositories the organisation supplies for reuse. The project adds to them at closure.
Information absorbed by overhearing in a shared workspace. One of the practical arguments for colocation.
Two people working at one workstation, giving continuous review and shared knowledge for the cost of some throughput.
Estimating from a statistical relationship, typically a rate multiplied by a quantity. Accurate to the extent the rate is.
A histogram of defect causes ordered by frequency, used to find the few causes producing most of the problems.
How long until cumulative returns cover the investment. Simple, widely used, and blind to everything that happens afterwards.
The scope, schedule and cost baselines combined, against which execution is measured.
The fourth Tuckman stage, where the team is effective, largely self-managing and handles its own conflict.
The monitoring process where every change request is reviewed and decided, and the decision propagated everywhere it matters.
The planning process that prioritises risks by assessed probability and impact. Subjective, fast, and done on every project.
The planning process that numerically analyses the combined effect of risks on overall objectives. The only optional risk process.
A concrete fictional user used to keep requirements anchored to a real need rather than an abstract role.
A three-point estimate weighting the most likely case four times: (O + 4M + P) / 6. Standard deviation is (P - O) / 6.
The worst-case estimate in a three-point technique, assuming the identified things go wrong.
A review at the end of a phase where the project is authorised to continue, continue with changes, or stop.
The planning process that determines who needs what information, when, in what form and from whom.
The planning process that sets how costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed and controlled.
The planning process that documents procurement decisions, specifies the approach and identifies potential sellers.
The planning process that identifies applicable quality requirements and how compliance will be demonstrated.
The planning process that defines how to estimate, acquire, manage and release both team and physical resources.
The planning process that sets how risk work will be conducted, including the probability and impact definitions everything downstream relies on.
The planning process that develops options, selects strategies and assigns owners for prioritised risks.
The planning process that establishes the policies and procedures for developing, managing and controlling the schedule.
The planning process that documents how scope will be defined, validated and controlled. Produces two plans, including the requirements management plan.
The planning process that develops approaches for involving stakeholders based on their needs, expectations and potential impact.
The budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be finished by now. Read off the cost baseline and fixed once the baseline is set.
The process group holding 24 of the 49 processes. Every knowledge area plans how it will work before planning its content.
Relative estimating where team members reveal estimates simultaneously and discuss the outliers. The discussion is the output; the number is a by-product.
In a fixed price incentive contract, the cost level above which the seller absorbs every further pound. PTA = ((ceiling - target price) / buyer share) + target cost.
Projects, programmes and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives. Its components need not be related to each other.
A two-axis classification of stakeholders that produces four engagement strategies: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
Network construction using nodes for activities and arrows for relationships, supporting FS, SS, FF and SF links.
How tightly repeated measurements cluster together. Independent of accuracy, which is closeness to the true value.
Scope, time and cost determined early and delivery made once at the end. Suits stable requirements and expensive late change.
An action taken to reduce the probability of negative consequences from a risk that has not yet occurred.
A grid mapping assessed probability against assessed impact to produce a priority rating for each risk.
A grouping of processes by the kind of work they do: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing. Not phases.
How procurement will be conducted: contract types, metrics, constraints, assumptions and the roles involved.
The description of what is being bought, detailed enough for sellers to price and for performance to be judged.
The single ordered source of work for a product, owned by the product owner. One list, one owner, one order.
The single person accountable for maximising product value and for ordering the backlog. A role held by one person, not a committee.
A time-oriented view of intended product direction at a coarser grain than the backlog, used for stakeholder alignment.
The features and functions of the product itself. Project scope is the work required to deliver it.
Related projects and activities managed together for benefits not available from managing them individually.
Adding detail to plans as more becomes known. Not the same as informal change: baselines still move only through change control.
A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary and unique are what separate it from operations.
The working days and shifts available for scheduled activities, distinct from individual resource calendars.
The tools and systems used to gather, integrate and distribute project information.
An organisational structure that standardises governance and shares resources and methods. Supportive, controlling or directive, in ascending order of authority.
The integrated document describing how the project is executed, monitored and closed. Includes every subsidiary plan and the three baselines.
The description of project and product scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria and explicit exclusions.
A structure where teams are dedicated to projects and the project manager holds most or all of the authority.
A working model produced to elicit feedback on requirements before committing to build. Cheapest way to resolve ambiguity.
Information placed where recipients retrieve it themselves. Suits large volumes and large audiences.
Information sent to specific recipients. Confirms delivery, never comprehension.
The degree to which a deliverable meets its requirements. Distinct from grade, which is a category of feature.
A structured review of whether processes and procedures are being followed and are producing the intended result.
How applicable policies and standards will be implemented, and how compliance will be shown.
Specific attributes to be measured and the tolerance permitted on each. Written before there is anything to measure.
A responsibility assignment matrix with four roles: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed. Exactly one accountable per row.
Improving the internal structure of work without changing its external behaviour. Maintenance of the ability to keep going fast.
Examining the relationship between variables to understand what drove an outcome. Used in closing to learn from project performance.
A set of increments made available to users. May contain many iterations, and need not coincide with a sprint boundary.
A condition or capability a solution must have to satisfy an agreement or standard. Stated so that it can be tested.
How requirements will be analysed, documented, traced and managed. Output of Plan Scope Management alongside the scope management plan.
Links each requirement to its origin and forward to the deliverable and test that satisfy it. Makes orphaned scope visible.
Assessing whether remaining contingency and management reserve remain proportionate to remaining risk exposure.
The exposure that remains after a response has been implemented. Accepted explicitly rather than ignored.
A hierarchical view of resources by category and type. Shares its acronym with the risk breakdown structure, which is a different thing.
When each resource is available, including shifts, holidays and competing commitments.
Adjusting start and finish dates so demand does not exceed availability. Can extend the schedule and change the critical path.
Adjusting activities within their float to even out demand. Never changes the critical path, and cannot always achieve the target.
A grid mapping work packages to the people or groups responsible for them. RACI is the most familiar form.
A recurring inspection of how the team works, ending in a committed improvement. Its output is a change, not a list of complaints.
Action to make a nonconforming component conform. Its volume is a measure of the process, not of the individuals.
An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, affects an objective. May be a threat or an opportunity. Future tense throughout.
The degree of uncertainty an organisation is willing to accept in anticipation of a reward.
A hierarchical categorisation of potential sources of risk, used to structure identification and to spot categories nobody has considered.
The record of identified risks with their assessments, owners, responses and status. Opened in Identify Risks and maintained throughout.
The view of overall project risk and the summary of individual risks, as distinct from the register's item-by-item detail.
The level of exposure above which action is required. Set in Plan Risk Management, and what makes a rating actionable.
Planning near-term work in detail and later work at a coarse level, elaborating as it approaches. A form of progressive elaboration.
Working backwards from a symptom to the underlying cause, so the fix prevents recurrence rather than treating the instance.
Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean on a control chart signals a process out of control, even if every point sits inside the limits.
Classifies stakeholders by power, urgency and legitimacy, which distinguishes the loud from the consequential.
Plots two variables against each other to show whether a relationship exists. Correlation, not causation.
The approved version of the schedule model, changed only through formal change control.
Shortening the schedule without reducing scope, by crashing (adds cost) or fast tracking (adds risk).
EV divided by PV. Tends toward 1.0 as a project completes regardless of lateness, so it is unreliable late on.
EV minus PV, expressed in currency rather than time. Negative means behind schedule.
The approved scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary and work packages taken together.
Uncontrolled expansion of scope without corresponding adjustment to time, cost or resources. A Control Scope failure.
A framework with three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts, built on transparency, inspection and adaptation.
Accountable for the team's effectiveness: coaches, removes impediments and protects the process. Does not assign work or collect status.
A coordination pattern where representatives from several teams meet to surface and resolve cross-team impediments.
A new risk created by implementing a response to another risk. Identified and assessed like any other.
A team that decides internally how to accomplish its work rather than being directed. What is done is still set outside the team.
Determining which uncertain inputs most affect an outcome. Usually presented as a tornado diagram, widest bar at the top.
Leading by serving the team: removing impediments, growing people and building the environment rather than directing tasks.
The opportunity response that brings in a partner better placed to capture the upside. The mirror of transfer.
The conflict mode that emphasises agreement and plays down the difference. Preserves the relationship, defers the issue.
The published basis on which seller proposals will be evaluated. Published before proposals arrive, or the evaluation is not defensible.
The boundaries of acceptability set by the customer. Distinct from control limits, which are derived from the process.
The person or group providing resources and support, and the one who issues the charter. Sits outside the project, above the project manager.
A fixed-length timebox of one month or less in which a usable increment is produced. Length does not change to accommodate unfinished work.
The sprint goal, the selected items and the plan for delivering them. Owned and managed by the developers.
The single objective for a sprint, which gives the team room to negotiate scope while keeping the commitment intact.
The event that starts a sprint, producing the sprint goal, the selected backlog items and a plan. Timeboxed to eight hours for a month-long sprint.
The event where the increment is inspected with stakeholders and the backlog adapted. A working session, not a demonstration.
Anyone who can affect, be affected by, or perceive themselves to be affected by the project. Perception counts.
Records current and desired engagement across unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive and leading. The gap is the plan.
The record of identified stakeholders, their interest, influence, expectations and classification. Updated continuously.
A measure of dispersion around the mean. In PERT it is (P - O) / 6, and variance is the square of it.
A narrative description of products or services to be supplied. The project version describes the project's own output; the procurement version describes what is bought.
Inspecting a selected subset rather than the whole population. Sample size and frequency are set in quality planning.
The second Tuckman stage: disagreement about approach, roles and authority. A stage to work through, not a failure to suppress.
A unit of relative size combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. Meaningful only within one team and never comparable between teams.
A matrix where the project manager holds moderate to high authority and there is usually a manager of project managers.
Examining strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats to broaden risk identification beyond the obvious.
Knowledge held as experience and intuition, transferred person to person rather than through documents. The half a wiki page cannot carry.
Deliberately selecting the processes, inputs, tools and life cycle that suit this project. A documented decision, not an omission.
The pace at which units must be produced to meet demand: available time divided by units required. Demand-driven, not capacity-driven.
The team's own working agreements: values, meeting norms, decision rules and the conflict process, written while the team is calm.
The accumulated cost of shortcuts taken to go faster now. Carries interest, paid in slowing delivery.
Writing a failing test before the work that satisfies it, so the requirement is expressed executably before it is built.
A risk with a negative effect on objectives. Responses are escalate, avoid, transfer, mitigate and accept.
Estimating from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values. Triangular averages them equally; beta or PERT weights the most likely four times.
Items completed per unit of time. With WIP it determines cycle time under Little's Law.
An agreed rate per unit of effort plus materials. Fast to put in place, and open-ended unless a not-to-exceed cap is set.
A fixed period that does not extend. Scope flexes to fit the box; the box never flexes to fit the scope.
The cost performance the remaining work must achieve to hit a target. Above about 1.10 it is generally regarded as unachievable.
The usual presentation of sensitivity analysis: horizontal bars ordered by influence, the widest at the top.
How long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish. Zero on the critical path.
The threat response that moves the financial impact to a third party through insurance, warranty, bond or contract. The risk still exists.
Examining performance over time to project where it is heading. Answers whether a variance is noise or a direction.
Observable signs that a risk is about to occur or has occurred. Without one, a contingent response cannot fire.
Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning. Teams move backwards when membership changes, which is normal.
A short statement of a need from a user's point of view, written to start a conversation rather than to replace one.
The monitoring process where the customer formally accepts completed deliverables. External and about signatures, where Control Quality is internal and about conformance.
Mapping the steps from request to delivery, distinguishing value-adding time from waiting. Usually reveals that most of the elapsed time is queue.
Comparing actual performance against the baseline and examining the size, cause and direction of the difference.
BAC minus EAC. The forecast overrun or underrun at the end of the project.
Story points completed per sprint by one team. A capacity planning input, never a productivity comparison between teams.
Deliverables that have passed Control Quality. The input Validate Scope requires; nothing unverified should reach the customer.
A team working across locations with limited or no face-to-face contact. Needs deliberate design of communication to approach colocated performance.
A structured method for turning what customers actually need into technical requirements.
The detail behind each WBS element: description, acceptance criteria, assumptions, responsible party and schedule and cost information.
A matrix where the project manager's role is closer to coordination and the functional manager retains resource control.
Evaluating scenarios to see their effect on the schedule, and to prepare for the ones that would hurt.
The conflict mode that retreats from the issue. Lowest-scoring in general, but correct when the issue is trivial or tempers need time.
A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into deliverables. The 100% rule says the children of a node sum to exactly that node.
Items started but not finished. Limiting it is the central mechanism of Kanban and the lever in Little's Law.
The lowest level of the WBS, small enough to estimate, schedule, budget and assign to one owner.
Raw observations from executing the work: dates, costs, counts. Produced only in Direct and Manage Project Work.
Data compared to the baseline and given meaning. Produced by the controlling processes.
Information compiled into a form for a decision or an audience. Produced by Monitor and Control Project Work.
An unplanned response to a risk that has already occurred and had no prepared response. Distinct from a contingency plan, which was prepared.

formulas.label: Earned value — the core four
formulas.blurb: Three measured inputs and everything derived from them. Write EV down first: it appears in all four of the variances and indices.

items.name: Planned value
items.where: BAC is the budget at completion; the percentage is the fraction of the plan that should be finished by now.
items.reads: The budgeted cost of the work that was scheduled to be done by this date.

items.name: Earned value
items.where: The percentage is physical progress, not effort burnt.
items.reads: The budgeted cost of the work actually finished. Value earned, priced at the plan.
items.trap: Percent complete means work delivered. A team that has spent 80% of the money has not thereby earned 80% of the value.

items.name: Actual cost
items.where: Measured from the accounts, not derived.
items.reads: What the finished work actually cost.

items.name: Cost variance
items.where: Both in currency.
items.reads: Negative is over budget. The figure is the overspend in pounds on the work done so far.
items.trap: Variances subtract and indices divide, and both put EV first. CV = AC − EV inverts every sign.

items.name: Schedule variance
items.where: Both in currency, even though this measures schedule.
items.reads: Negative is behind schedule, expressed as the budget value of the missing work.
items.trap: SV is in pounds, not days. It also collapses to zero at the end of a late project, because EV and PV both reach BAC.

items.name: Cost performance index
items.where: Dimensionless.
items.reads: Work earned per pound spent. Below 1.00 is over budget; 0.85 means 85p of value for every pound.

items.name: Schedule performance index
items.where: Dimensionless.
items.reads: Progress rate against plan. Below 1.00 is behind; 0.90 means nine tenths of the planned pace.

items.name: Percent complete and percent spent
items.expr:
% complete = EV ÷ BAC
% spent    = AC ÷ BAC
items.where: Both against the original budget.
items.reads: The gap between the two is the cost problem stated as a percentage.

formulas.label: Forecasting and recovery
formulas.blurb: Where the project lands, and what it would take to change that. Choosing the right EAC is a judgement about the cause of the variance, not an arithmetic step.

items.name: EAC — variances are typical
items.where: The default when nothing in the question says otherwise.
items.reads: Projects the efficiency achieved so far across all the remaining work.
items.trap: This is the right choice when the overrun is systemic. If the overrun came from a one-off event that will not recur, it overstates the finish.

items.name: EAC — variance was a one-off
items.where: BAC − EV is the remaining work at budgeted rates.
items.reads: Sunk cost stays sunk; everything still to do is added at plan.
items.trap: Look for wording like a one-time event, a settled dispute, or a supplier problem now fixed.

items.name: EAC — cost and schedule both bite
items.where: The denominator is sometimes weighted, e.g. 0.8 CPI + 0.2 SPI.
items.reads: Used when the recovery must hold a deadline as well as a budget, so lateness costs money.
items.trap: Only reach for this when the question ties the two together. Unprompted, it produces a pessimistic answer that is not among the options.

items.name: EAC — the plan is no longer credible
items.where: ETC re-estimated from scratch by the people doing the work.
items.reads: The original baseline is abandoned as a predictor and the remainder is re-estimated.
items.trap: Correct when the question says the original assumptions are invalid; a re-estimate, not a calculation.

items.name: Estimate to complete
items.where: Currency.
items.reads: What the rest of the project is forecast to cost from today.

items.name: Variance at completion
items.where: Currency.
items.reads: Negative means the project is forecast to finish over budget by that amount.

items.name: TCPI against the original budget
items.where: Remaining work over remaining money.
items.reads: The efficiency the team must now hit to finish on the original budget. Above 1.00 means they must work better than they have been.

items.name: TCPI against the revised budget
items.where: Same numerator, revised denominator.
items.reads: The efficiency needed to hit the new forecast instead of the old baseline.
items.trap: Both TCPI formulas are remaining work over remaining money. Change the target and only the denominator moves.

formulas.label: Estimating and PERT
formulas.blurb: Three-point estimating, the spread around the mean, and how spread accumulates along a path.

items.name: PERT / beta expected duration
items.where: O optimistic, M most likely, P pessimistic.
items.reads: A weighted mean that pulls the answer towards the most likely value.
items.trap: Divide by 6, not 3, and only after multiplying M by 4. The weights must sum to the divisor.

items.name: Triangular expected duration
items.where: The straight average of the three.
items.reads: Used where there is no reason to trust the most likely value more than the extremes.
items.trap: A question that says simple average or triangular wants this one; PERT and beta want the weighted version.

items.name: Standard deviation
items.where: Only the two extremes; M plays no part.
items.reads: The spread of the estimate. A wide gap between optimistic and pessimistic means an uncertain estimate.

items.name: Variance
items.where: The square of the standard deviation.
items.reads: The form that can be added up. Standard deviations cannot be summed; variances can.

items.name: Confidence ranges
items.where: Assumes the estimate is roughly normal.
items.reads: Quote a commitment at 2σ or 3σ, not at the mean: the mean is a coin toss.

items.name: Rolling up a path
items.expr:
Path tE = Σ tE
Path σ  = √(Σ σ²)
items.where: Sum the means; sum the variances, then take the root.
items.reads: Path uncertainty grows more slowly than path length, because the variances add and the root shrinks the total.
items.trap: Adding the standard deviations along a path is the classic error and always overstates the spread.

formulas.label: Communication channels
formulas.blurb: One formula, and the reason it appears so often is that the growth is quadratic and people underestimate it.

items.name: Number of channels
items.where: n is everyone who communicates, the project manager included.
items.reads: Lines of communication in a group of n people.
items.trap: Forgetting to count yourself is the most common slip. If a question adds people to a team, count both totals and subtract.

items.name: Channels added by growth
items.where: n₁ before, n₂ after.
items.reads: The new channels created. Adding three people to a team of seven adds 24 channels, not three.

formulas.label: Risk and decision analysis
formulas.blurb: Expected monetary value, and the roll-up that turns a tree of options into one number per branch.

items.name: Expected monetary value
items.where: Impact carries a sign: threats negative, opportunities positive.
items.reads: The average outcome if this risk were faced many times.
items.trap: The sign convention is the mark. A threat with a 30% chance of costing 40,000 is an EMV of −12,000, not 12,000.

items.name: Contingency reserve
items.expr: Reserve = Σ EMV of the identified risks
items.where: Across the register, threats and opportunities together.
items.reads: The contingency for known risks. Management reserve for unknown risks sits outside this and outside the cost baseline.
items.trap: Contingency is inside the cost baseline and the project manager controls it. Management reserve is neither.

items.name: Decision tree roll-up
items.expr:
At a chance node    : EMV = Σ (P × payoff)
At a decision node  : take the best branch EMV
Net path value      : EMV − cost of that branch
items.where: Work right to left, from the payoffs back to the first decision.
items.reads: The branch with the best net value is the recommendation.
items.trap: Subtract the branch's own cost once, at the branch, and never subtract it again inside each outcome. Probabilities at one chance node must total 1.0.

items.name: Value of perfect information
items.expr: EVPI = EMV with perfect information − best EMV without it
items.where: The first term picks the best payoff for each state, then weights by probability.
items.reads: The most a rational buyer would pay for a study that removes the uncertainty entirely.

formulas.label: Procurement and incentive contracts
formulas.blurb: The point of total assumption, and the sharing arithmetic on either side of it.

items.name: Point of total assumption
items.expr: PTA = ((Ceiling price − Target price) ÷ Buyer share) + Target cost
items.where: Target price is target cost plus target fee. Buyer share is the buyer's fraction of an overrun.
items.reads: The actual cost at which the seller starts absorbing every further pound. Above it the seller's fee falls pound for pound.
items.trap: The divisor is the buyer's share, not the seller's, and the addend is the target cost, not the target price. Both are easy to swap under time pressure.

items.name: Final fee under an FPIF
items.expr: Fee = Target fee + (Target cost − Actual cost) × Seller share
items.where: The bracket is positive on an underrun and negative on an overrun.
items.reads: Come in under target and the seller keeps their share of the saving; overrun and they fund their share of it.
items.trap: The share ratio is quoted buyer/seller. In an 80/20 the seller keeps 20% of a saving and funds 20% of an overrun.

items.name: Final price
items.expr: Price = Actual cost + Fee,  capped at the ceiling
items.where: The cap binds at and above the PTA.
items.reads: Never more than the ceiling price, whatever the actual cost reaches.
items.trap: Apply the cap last. A computed price above the ceiling is not the answer; the ceiling is.

items.name: Sharing a saving or an overrun
items.expr:
Buyer share  = Variance × buyer fraction
Seller share = Variance × seller fraction
items.where: Variance is target cost minus actual cost.
items.reads: Both fractions apply to the same variance and must total 1.0.

formulas.label: Network, float and the critical path
formulas.blurb: The passes are bookkeeping; the marks are in the float. This sheet uses day numbering, where the first activity starts on day 1.

items.name: Forward pass — earliest dates
items.expr:
ES = max(EF of predecessors) + 1
EF = ES + Duration − 1
items.where: A starting activity has ES = 1.
items.reads: Left to right through the network. The largest EF at the end is the project duration.
items.trap: The ±1 belongs to day numbering, where an activity of 3 days starting on day 1 finishes on day 3. If a question numbers from day 0, both adjustments disappear.

items.name: Backward pass — latest dates
items.expr:
LF = min(LS of successors) − 1
LS = LF − Duration + 1
items.where: A finishing activity has LF = the project duration.
items.reads: Right to left. Take the minimum, not the maximum: the constraint is the earliest successor.

items.name: Total float
items.where: Both forms give the same number; use whichever pair you have.
items.reads: How long the activity can slip before the project end date moves.
items.trap: Total float belongs to the path, not the activity. Consuming it on one activity removes it from every other activity on that path.

items.name: Free float
items.where: Zero for any activity feeding straight into a critical successor.
items.reads: How long the activity can slip before it delays any successor's early start.
items.trap: Free float is never greater than total float, and a merge point is where the two most often differ.

items.name: Critical path
items.expr: The longest path through the network; every activity on it has TF = 0
items.where: There can be more than one.
items.reads: The shortest possible project duration. Longest path, shortest schedule.
items.trap: Near-critical paths matter: a path with two days of float becomes critical after a three-day slip, and the answer to a delay question changes with it.

items.name: Crash cost slope
items.expr: Slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) ÷ (Normal duration − Crash duration)
items.where: Cost per period saved.
items.reads: Crash the cheapest slope first, and only on the critical path.
items.trap: Crashing a non-critical activity buys nothing. After each crash, recheck which path is longest.

formulas.label: Business case and selection
formulas.blurb: The figures a sponsor uses to choose between projects. In every one of them, bigger is better except payback, where sooner is better.

items.name: Present value
items.where: r is the discount rate per period, n the number of periods.
items.reads: What a future sum is worth today.

items.name: Net present value
items.where: Cₜ is the cash flow in period t, C₀ the initial outlay.
items.reads: Positive means the project earns more than the discount rate. Choose the higher NPV.
items.trap: NPV is already net of the investment, so no further deduction is made. Comparing NPVs never needs the durations.

items.name: Internal rate of return
items.expr: The rate r at which NPV = 0
items.where: Solved iteratively, not in closed form.
items.reads: The project's own rate of return. Higher is better, and above the cost of capital is the test.
items.trap: Nothing on the exam asks you to compute an IRR by hand. It asks you to compare two, or to read it against a hurdle rate.

items.name: Payback period
items.expr: PB = full years before recovery + (outstanding ÷ cash flow in the recovery year)
items.where: Undiscounted unless the question says otherwise.
items.reads: How long until the investment is recovered. Shorter is better.
items.trap: Payback ignores everything after the recovery date and ignores the time value of money entirely, which is why it is never the only criterion.

items.name: Return on investment
items.where: Usually quoted as a percentage.
items.reads: Return per unit invested.

items.name: Benefit–cost ratio
items.where: Both discounted, if the question discounts either.
items.reads: Above 1.0 means the benefits exceed the costs.
items.trap: A BCR of 0.8 is a loss-making project even though the number is positive. Compare against 1.0, not against zero.

items.name: Opportunity cost
items.expr: Opportunity cost = value of the best option not taken
items.where: The runner-up, not the sum of the rejected options.
items.reads: Choosing a project worth 500,000 over one worth 350,000 carries an opportunity cost of 350,000.

formulas.label: Agile and flow metrics
formulas.blurb: Empirical measures taken from what the team actually finished. Little's Law ties three of them together and is the one worth being able to rearrange.

items.name: Velocity
items.where: Averaged over the last few iterations, typically three.
items.reads: The team's demonstrated rate. Used for forecasting, never for comparison between teams.
items.trap: Only accepted work counts. Points for a story that is nearly done contribute nothing this iteration.

items.name: Iterations remaining
items.where: Round up.
items.reads: The forecast, as a range if velocity varies.

items.name: Throughput
items.expr: Throughput = items completed ÷ unit of time
items.where: Items, not points.
items.reads: How fast finished work leaves the system.

items.name: Cycle time
items.where: Measured per item, then averaged.
items.reads: How long an item takes once someone starts it.

items.name: Lead time
items.where: Starts when the customer asks, not when the team starts.
items.reads: What the customer experiences. Always at least the cycle time, and usually much longer.
items.trap: Lead time includes queue time before work starts, so it is the larger of the two. Reducing WIP shortens both.

items.name: Little's Law
items.expr:
Cycle time = WIP ÷ Throughput

WIP        = Throughput × Cycle time
Throughput = WIP ÷ Cycle time
items.where: Holds for a stable system over a period long enough to average out.
items.reads: The mathematical case for limiting work in progress: halve the WIP at a fixed throughput and you halve the cycle time.
items.trap: The units must agree. WIP in items and throughput in items per week give a cycle time in weeks.

items.name: Takt time
items.where: Demand-driven, not capacity-driven.
items.reads: The pace the customer requires, against which the actual pace is compared.
